title: The Barry Manilow T-shirt
hook: Students in an embarrassing T-shirt guessed half the room noticed. Few did.
peek: Psychologists at Cornell had students walk into a room wearing a T-shirt with Barry Manilow's face on it. The wearers guessed that about half the people there would notice. In fact only about a quarter did.
lede: In a 2000 study at Cornell University, Thomas Gilovich and colleagues asked students to put on a T-shirt showing the singer Barry Manilow, chosen because the students found it embarrassing. Each walked into a room of peers, stayed briefly, then left. The wearers guessed that about half the room had noticed the shirt. Only about a quarter of people had.

bullets.text: The researchers picked Manilow after checking that students saw his face on a shirt as unfashionable. The point was to make the wearer feel conspicuous, and it worked: they expected far more attention than they got.
Gilovich, Victoria Medvec and Kenneth Savitsky called this the spotlight effect: we feel as if a spotlight follows us, so we overestimate how much others notice our looks and slips.
The researchers argued that we start from our own vivid sense of how we look and adjust too little for the fact that everyone else is busy thinking about themselves.
In a follow-up, students wore shirts showing people they admired. They still overestimated how many noticed, so the effect is not only about embarrassment.
